subject: Agriculture
title: Soybeans Rule the World
description: One-minute skill: Soybeans Rule the World.

hook.text: Soybeans contain 40% protein and 20% oil—no other crop delivers both at this scale.

buildup.text: Originally from China, soybeans conquered global agriculture after World War II as demand for feed and oil soared.

discovery.text: The US and Brazil now produce 70% of the world's soybeans. It's their most valuable export crop.

twist.text: Most soybeans aren't eaten by people—they're crushed for oil and the leftover meal feeds livestock.

climax.text: Soybean expansion is the leading driver of tropical deforestation in South America.

punchline.text: The world's most versatile crop is also one of its most destructive.

quiz.question: What is the primary use of the global soybean harvest?
options: Crushed for oil and the meal used as animal feed

details.summary: Soybeans are the world's most important oilseed and protein crop, dominating global trade. This topic covers soybean cultivation, their role in animal feed and food products, and the environmental consequences of relentless expansion.
details.whyItMatters: Global meat consumption depends on soybean meal for livestock feed. Soy expansion drives deforestation in the Amazon and Cerrado, making it a flashpoint where agriculture meets environmentalism.
takeaways: Soybeans provide about 70% of the world's protein meal for livestock feed
Brazil has overtaken the US as the world's largest soy producer
Soy expansion in South America has cleared millions of hectares of forest and savanna

faq.question: Why are soybeans so dominant in global agriculture?
faq.answer: Soybeans are uniquely versatile: they contain both high protein (about 36%) and high oil (about 20%). Soybean meal feeds most of the world's poultry, pigs, and farmed fish, while soy oil is the second most consumed vegetable oil globally.

faq.question: How does soybean farming affect deforestation?
faq.answer: Rising global demand for soy—primarily for animal feed—has driven massive clearing of tropical forests and savannas in Brazil, Argentina, and Paraguay. The Cerrado biome has lost over half its native vegetation, largely to soy expansion.
